title: Causality-Aware Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations
summary: Attacks the feature-independence assumption in local post-hoc explanation by learning a causal graph over the data first and sampling the local neighbourhood along it, so that the perturbed instances LIME queries the black box with respect the dependencies present in the real data. SDV supplies the statistical machinery for judging that neighbourhood: the paper adopts its Gaussian mixture log-likelihood, inverted Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic and its binned approximation of continuous KL divergence to compare generated instances against the real distribution, and notes that a prior method used CTGAN for the same neighbourhood-realism purpose.
evidence: the evaluation section states the paper exploits the statistical measures outlined in SDV, specifically the Gaussian Mixture Log Likelihood and the Inverted Kolmogorov-Smirnov D statistic, and describes how the SDV framework approximates continuous KL divergence by binning continuous values before computing relative entropy; the related-work section notes that another approach uses a Conditional Tabular GAN to generate more realistic synthetic data for querying the model being explained

title: Comparing the Utility and Disclosure Risk of Synthetic Data with Samples of Microdata
summary: Puts synthetic data and conventional sampled microdata on the same risk-utility map, so that a data custodian can ask whether releasing a synthetic file is better or worse than releasing a sample, and applies the framework to four census microdata sets. CTGAN is one of the three synthesisers whose output is measured, pinned at version 0.4.3 and run five times per dataset under different random seeds; the paper also credits its mode-specific normalization for handling non-Gaussian and multimodal columns and varies the differential-privacy parameter across its runs.
evidence: the introduction states the experiments used four census microdata sets with synthetic data generated by three state-of-the-art methods, CTGAN, Synthpop and DataSynthesizer; section 2.2 credits CTGAN by Xu et al. with mode-specific normalisation to overcome non-Gaussian and multimodal distributions; section 3.1 records that version 0.4.3 of CTGAN was used for all experiments and that five models were created per dataset under different random seeds

title: ConvGeN: Convex space learning improves deep-generative oversampling for tabular imbalanced classification on smaller datasets
summary: Argues that deep oversamplers trained adversarially need more data than small imbalanced tables provide, and proposes ConvGeN, which learns convex combinations of minority neighbourhoods so that generated points stay inside the convex space of the minority class and remain separable from the majority. CTGAN is one of the two tabular generators it is measured against: the paper runs it from the sdv-dev repository, describes its conditional vector and packing discriminator, and automates the discrete-versus-continuous column declaration it requires, reporting that on smaller datasets CTGAN performs worse than the non-generative baseline.
affiliations: University of Rostock; Leibniz Institute for Food Systems Biology
evidence: section IV.D gives the CTGAN git link as github.com/sdv-dev/CTGAN and describes its non-Gaussian modelling, conditional vector and packing discriminator; the same section states that to train CTGAN a list of discrete columns must be supplied and that the authors automated this decision by integer-versus-fractional column typing; the results report that CTGAN and CTAB-GAN in most cases perform worse than the baseline on smaller tabular datasets

title: Data-IQ: Characterizing subgroups with heterogeneous outcomes in tabular data
summary: Separates a training set into easy, ambiguous and hard examples by tracking each example's predictive confidence and aleatoric uncertainty across training epochs, so that irreducible label noise can be told apart from model-side uncertainty and subgroups with heterogeneous outcomes surfaced. One experiment applies this to choosing between synthetic datasets: CTGAN and Gaussian Copula stand in for two synthetic data vendors, both run from the sdv-dev implementation, and the paper reports that the generator producing the higher proportion of easy examples is the one whose data trains the better real-data classifier.
affiliations: University of Oxford; Alan Turing Institute
University of Cambridge; Alan Turing Institute; University of California, Los Angeles
evidence: the appendix on principled dataset comparison states that two synthetic datasets are compared using two models representing two synthetic data vendors, namely CTGAN and Gaussian Copula, with implementations taken from github.com/sdv-dev/SDV; Table 1 ranks the CTGAN and Gaussian Copula datasets by accuracy and by proportion of easy examples across the Prostate, Covid, Support and Fetal datasets

title: Design Target Achievement Index: A Differentiable Metric to Enhance Deep Generative Models in Multi-Objective Inverse Design
summary: Observes that deep generative models in engineering design optimise for statistical resemblance to the training set rather than for meeting a designer's targets, and proposes the Design Target Achievement Index, a differentiable score over multiple objectives and constraints that can be added to a generative model's loss so that sampling is steered toward feasible designs that hit the targets. CTGAN and TVAE are the two tabular generators it benchmarks against on parametric bicycle-frame data, chosen as the established state of the art for the GAN and VAE classes respectively.
evidence: the abstract reports comparative performance against baseline deep generative models including specialized tabular generation algorithms like the Conditional Tabular GAN; the methods section states the paper tests TVAE and CTGAN introduced by Xu et al. in 2019, noting both established state-of-the-art performance on tabular data generation for their respective model classes

title: FCT-GAN: Enhancing Table Synthesis via Fourier Transform
summary: Argues that tabular GANs miss correlations spanning the whole row and are sensitive to the order in which columns are presented, and proposes FCT-GAN, which tokenizes each encoded row with a CNN filter and then passes the tokens through Fourier network blocks in both generator and discriminator so that learnable weights over all frequencies capture global column relations. The paper first demonstrates the permutation problem empirically across three column orders, then reports the smallest variation for its own model. CTGAN and TVAE are two of the five synthesizers it benchmarks throughout, and the conditional vector FCT-GAN adopts is the one the paper attributes to CTGAN and describes as later improved by CTAB-GAN+, together with the variational Gaussian mixture encoding of continuous columns.
evidence: section II states that CT-GAN and CTAB-GAN improve synthesis through preprocessing steps and that the conditional vector was designed by CT-GAN and later improved by CTAB-GAN, reducing mode collapse on minority categories; section IV.B.2 adopts that conditional vector and the variational Gaussian mixture encoder for continuous columns from CTAB-GAN+; Tables I, III and IV report CT-GAN and TVAE among the five baselines across seven datasets and three column orders; Table V records that CT-GAN and TVAE could not be trained on the Youth dataset because of conditional vector dimensionality

title: FinGAN: Generative Adversarial Network for Analytical Customer Relationship Management in Banking and Insurance
summary: Attacks class imbalance in banking and insurance analytics two ways: oversampling the minority class with a GAN, and a hybrid that first reduces the majority class to the support vectors found by a one-class SVM before oversampling, tested on churn prediction, auto insurance fraud and loan default with six classifiers and a statistical significance test. CTGAN is one of the three generators run unmodified as the oversampler, and the paper's conclusion rests on it: it forms a headline column of the results tables for all three datasets and the CTGAN-based approaches are the ones reported as best.
affiliations: Institute for Development and Research in Banking Technology; University of Hyderabad
Institute for Development and Research in Banking Technology
evidence: The abstract states Vanilla GAN, Wasserstein GAN and CTGAN are each employed to oversample the minority class; section 3.3.1 states CTGAN was used to produce synthetic data with no changes to its architecture; section 5 attributes CTGAN's superiority over the other two to mode-specific normalization for multiple modes in continuous variables and to training by sampling with conditional generators for unbalanced categorical variables; Tables 7, 9 and 11 give CTGAN and CTGAN+OCSVM columns for churn, insurance fraud and loan default, with CTGAN plus xgboost reported at the best AUC of 0.874 on bank default; the conclusion states that CTGAN based approaches yielded best statistically significant results. pypdf renders some occurrences of the name as CTAGN

title: G2A2: An Automated Graph Generator with Attributes and Anomalies
summary: Addresses the shortage of dynamic attributed graph datasets carrying anomaly ground truth by generating them: a temporal bipartite graph is produced first, anomalies are injected to emulate burstiness and propagation, and node attributes are then synthesised and mapped onto the graph. CTGAN performs that last stage, run as two separate instances trained on the normal and anomalous partitions of a source table so that the attributes attached to injected anomalies come from the anomalous distribution.
evidence: the overview states that by leveraging deep generative models like CTGAN the pipeline generates and maps realistic attributes to the graph; the attribute-generation section states that two conditional tabular generative adversarial networks are used, with the source dataset divided into normal and anomalous parts so each instance learns the corresponding attribute distribution

title: Generating Synthetic Population
summary: Builds a synthetic population for India at several administrative levels by combining census, IHDS-II, NSS and gridded population sources, assigning individuals to households and households to administrative units so that the result can seed agent-based simulation. CTGAN is one of the generators trialled for producing the base population and is reported as rejected in favour of iterative proportional updating, on the ground that IPU can match individual-level and household-level characteristics simultaneously while CTGAN cannot.
evidence: the methods section names Iterative Proportional Fitting, Iterative Proportional Updating and a specialized neural network called Conditional-Tabular Generative Adversarial Network by Xu et al. as the techniques used to generate new data; a later passage states the authors also experimented with CTGAN to generate a base population and that the major advantage of IPU over CTGAN is IPU's ability to match individual-level and household-level characteristics at once

title: Generative Trees: Adversarial and Copycat
summary: Develops a tree-based generative model for tabular data, deriving a variational GAN-style loss whose tightness follows from the properness of the supervised loss and the calibration property that decision trees satisfy, and giving both a boosting-compliant adversarial training algorithm and a copycat scheme in which the generator copies the discriminator's tree at run time and completes it. CTGAN is the single neural contender the empirical case is argued against, run at 10, 300 and 1000 epochs across the train-on-synthetic, synthetic-versus-real discrimination and data-augmentation experiments, with per-domain statistical win/tie/loss counts against it reported in Tables 3 and 4.
evidence: the introduction states that on fake/real discrimination generative trees tend to get better results than the neural networks of CT-GAN, citing Xu et al. 2019; section 6.2 names CT-GAN as the state-of-the-art contender, trained for 10, 300 or 1000 epochs, with random forests and gradient-boosted trees fitted on real or fake data; Table 3 reports statistical wins/ties/losses for generative trees against CT-GAN across the TRAIN-SYNTH, SYNTH-DISCRIM and SYNTH-AUG protocols on 10 to 13 domains, and Table 4 plots per-domain accuracy with CT-GAN results marked by epoch count. Importance 3: CTGAN is a compared generator only - generative trees share none of its architecture, and the paper does not adopt its conditional vector or mode-specific normalization. Note the pypdf rendering is CT-GAN throughout, which the tight scan matches.

title: Improving Correlation Capture in Generating Imbalanced Data using Differentially Private Conditional GANs
summary: Proposes DP-CGANS, a conditional GAN for tabular data whose conditional vector is built to preserve correlations between variables rather than only marginal distributions, trained under differential privacy so that the synthetic records carry a stated privacy cost. Its continuous-column encoder is the mode-specific normalization proposed in the CTGAN paper, adopted directly; CTGAN is one of the three GAN frameworks it is measured against; and the whole comparison is run inside SDGym, the SDV project's benchmarking suite, which supplies the utility and privacy metrics reported.
evidence: the model section states that continuous variables are transformed using mode-specific normalization proposed by Xu et al., the CTGAN reference; the related-work section credits CTGAN with inventing training-by-sampling for imbalanced categorical variables alongside the conditional vector; section 4.1 compares DP-CGANS against CTGAN, MedGAN and TableGAN using the benchmarking suite developed by Synthetic Data Gym, footnoted to github.com/sdv-dev/SDGym, which supplies the data utility and privacy metrics

title: PromptEHR: Conditional Electronic Healthcare Records Generation with Prompt Learning
summary: Casts synthetic electronic health record generation as conditional language modelling: PromptEHR encodes a patient's demographics and prior visits as prompts to an encoder-decoder language model, so that longitudinal multimodal visit sequences can be generated and evaluated by perplexity rather than by tabular similarity alone. CTGAN is the tabular-generation prior art the design departs from, cited for the observation that GANs and VAEs struggle with multimodal non-Gaussian distributions and sparse one-hot vectors, and named among the conditional-GAN approaches that generate only static tabular records.
evidence: the introduction states that GANs and VAEs usually struggle to model complex multimodal and non-Gaussian distributions as well as sparse one-hot-encoded vectors, citing Xu et al. 2019; the related-work section lists conditional GANs, again citing Xu et al. 2019, among the EHR generation methods that produce only static tabular or single-modal longitudinal records, which is the limitation the language-model approach is proposed to remove

title: RCC-GAN: Regularized Compound Conditional GAN for Large-Scale Tabular Data Synthesis
summary: Replaces the per-column mask conditional vector of prior tabular GANs with a compound conditional vector that carries several columns at once, adds a regularization term over the fitted mixture parameters, and redesigns the continuous-column transformer so multivariate distributions survive encoding, targeting tables too wide for one-hot conditioning to remain tractable. CTGAN is the design the paper works from and against: it reproduces CTGAN's conditional vector definition in full before proposing its own, follows CTGAN in mapping discrete and binary columns through a tanh transformer, builds its continuous-column encoder on the same variational Gaussian mixture idea, takes the Gumbel softmax in its residual blocks from the CTGAN authors, and reports CTGAN as one of the GAN baselines it is measured against.
affiliations: Ecole de Technologie Superieure; Caisses Desjardins du Quebec
evidence: section III restates the CTGAN conditional vector as equation 10 and states that conditioning the generator on it significantly improves generalizability and stability; section IV notes that following CTGAN the paper also uses the tanh mapping for discrete and binary columns while designing a new VGM-based transformer for continuous ones; the residual-network section credits Xu et al. for the Gumbel softmax it adopts; the results tables report CTGAN alongside MotGAN, VeeGAN, ItsGAN, InvGAN and BctGAN as baselines

title: Sequential Models in the Synthetic Data Vault
summary: Documents the PAR algorithm used for multi-sequence time series in SDV: context columns are modeled separately from the sequence body, allowing generation of new entities with their own coherent sequences.
evidence: first-party: this artifact is SDV, not something that integrates it

title: Synthesising Electronic Health Records: Cystic Fibrosis Patient Group
summary: Synthesises cystic fibrosis electronic health records from the IBM Explorys dataset to address class imbalance in mortality-risk prediction, and evaluates four generators on authenticity, fidelity and diversity before using their samples to augment the minority class, finding that augmentation improves two of four downstream models while trading against similarity to the real records. CTGAN is one of the four compared generators, implemented from the architecture and code repository of Xu et al. (2019), and its behaviour on duplication, precision, density and coverage is reported alongside the variational autoencoder and the two differentially private GANs.
evidence: the Synthetic Data Generators paragraph in section 3 names the four generators as VAE, DPGAN at two noise levels and CTGAN, and describes CTGAN as addressing sparsity and imbalanced categorical columns by sampling vectors during training and conditioning the generator; the appendix states that CTGAN was implemented by adopting the model architecture provided in Xu et al. (2019) and the corresponding code repo; Figure 1 reports CTGAN duplicating 34 per cent of the training data across 100,000 samples and generating the largest number of unique samples at an average of 33,689; the fidelity paragraph records CTGAN last on precision (0.37) and density (0.13) but highest on recall (0.67), with coverage degrading to 0.31

title: Synthetic Data-Based Simulators for Recommender Systems: A Survey
summary: Surveys simulators that stand in for live recommender systems during development, decomposing them into four components — synthetic user and item profiles, a response function, a feedback loop, and an evaluation procedure — and comparing published simulators on which components each supplies and how each handles real-world drift in user behaviour. SDV is cited twice: as the library SynEvaRec calls to build synthetic user and item profiles with Gaussian Copula, CTGAN and CopulaGAN, and as a source of ready-made metrics for judging generated data quality, grouped into statistical, likelihood and detection families; the survey itself runs nothing.
evidence: section on synthetic profile generation states that SynEvaRec uses the existing library for synthetic data generation SDV (Patki et al. 2016) to create synthetic profiles of users and items with Gaussian Copula, CTGAN and CopulaGAN models; the evaluation component section proposes assessing synthetic data quality with metrics from the SDV library, divided into statistical, likelihood and detection groups; the SDV DSAA 2016 paper is the cited anchor and no experiment in the survey uses it

title: TabDDPM: Modelling Tabular Data with Diffusion Models
summary: Applies denoising diffusion to general tabular data by running Gaussian diffusion on the normalized continuous features and multinomial diffusion on the one-hot categorical features under a shared reverse model, and shows across a wide benchmark that the result beats the GAN and VAE alternatives on machine-learning efficiency and on marginal and correlation fidelity, with SMOTE the only competitive shallow method. CTGAN and TVAE are two of the compared generators, with TVAE described as the state-of-the-art tabular variational autoencoder and CTGAN as the best-known GAN-based synthesizer, and the paper's primary evaluation measure is the machine-learning efficiency protocol credited to Xu et al.
evidence: the baselines section names TVAE (Xu et al. 2019) as the state-of-the-art variational autoencoder for tabular data generation, with no VAE-like alternative that outperforms it and has public source, and CTGAN (Xu et al. 2019) as arguably the most popular and well-known GAN-based model for synthetic data generation; the evaluation-measure paragraph states that the primary measure is machine-learning efficiency, cited to Xu et al. 2019; Table 3 reports average ranks for CTGAN and TVAE alongside CTABGAN+, SMOTE and TabDDPM on Wasserstein distance, Jensen-Shannon divergence and correlation-matrix L2, and Figures 2-3 compare TVAE's feature distributions and correlations against TabDDPM's. Importance 3: compared generators plus an adopted evaluation protocol, with no reuse of the conditional vector or mode-specific normalization.

title: Causal-TGAN: Generating Tabular Data Using Causal Generative Adversarial Networks
summary: Introduces Causal-TGAN, a tabular generator that conditions generation on a causal graph over the columns so that samples follow the causal structure rather than the joint distribution alone, and reports performance close to the strongest baseline while requiring only a partial graph. CTGAN is the leading comparison generator, its Gaussian-mixture encoding of continuous columns is adopted for every model in the study, and all reported metrics are computed with the SDV package's single-table evaluation module.
evidence: section 4.1 states that implementations provided by the SDV package are used for all the metrics above, footnote 3 pointing to sdv.dev/SDV/user_guides/evaluation/single_table; section 4.2 compares Causal-TGAN against PrivBN, MedGAN, TableGAN and CTGAN at 300 epochs and batch size 500, states that the variables are encoded by the method proposed in Xu et al. (2019) with a Gaussian mixture model for continuous columns, and reports in Tables 2 and 3 that CTGAN ties for best average column similarity and is best on machine-learning efficacy for adult and news. Recorded api_user rather than baseline_only because running an SDV-family tool outranks the comparison role, following the DP-CGANS precedent

title: Conditional Generative Models for Counterfactual Explanations
summary: Proposes a framework that trains a conditional generative model to emit counterfactual explanations in a single forward pass rather than by per-instance optimization, conditioning the generator on the desired target prediction and applying it across image, time-series and mixed-type tabular modalities. The tabular branch, named CF-CTGAN, is built directly on CTGAN: the generator and discriminator architectures are reused as-is from Xu et al., continuous features carry CTGAN's mode-specific normalization and categorical features its Gumbel-Softmax sampling, with CTGAN's conditional vector removed and replaced by conditioning on the target class.
evidence: section 3.4 states that for tabular data the authors adapt the CTGAN approach and architecture, with fully connected generator and discriminator with residual connections, mode-specific normalization of continuous features, one-hot encoding of categoricals and Gumbel-Softmax for categorical sampling, and that they dispense with the use of conditional vectors; appendix A.3 states that the GCF and D architectures are directly reused as-is from Xu et al. and records mode-specific normalization applied to the Adult Census numerical variables; Figure 7 labels the method CF CTGAN (Ours) and Figures 15-16 caption the generated counterfactuals as produced by CF-CTGAN. The compared baselines are DiCE and CFProto, both counterfactual-search methods, so CTGAN is the substrate and not a benchmark.
needs: importance 5 follows the named-variant convention (CF-CTGAN reuses CTGAN's generator and discriminator as-is). Reviewable: the tabular branch is one of three modality branches (CelebA uses a ResNet encoder-decoder, ECG adapts RCGAN), so a reviewer applying the constrained-DGM precedent for a substrate that carries only part of the paper may prefer 4.

title: DTGAN: Differential Private Training for Tabular GANs
summary: Asks where differential privacy should be enforced in a tabular GAN, and answers it by building two variants of DTGAN that apply DP-SGD with subsampled Renyi accounting to the discriminator and to the generator respectively, showing that noising the discriminator gives the better utility-privacy trade-off and that DP-SGD outperforms the PATE framework on three datasets against PATE-GAN and DP-WGAN. CTGAN's conditional architecture is what the generator-side privacy argument rests on: the generator loss is described as a by-product of that architecture, which makes the conditional vector independent of the real training data, but CTGAN itself is neither run nor compared against.
evidence: section 3.1 states that the generator loss is a by-product of the conditional architecture and is used to ensure the generator respects the conditional constraints imposed during training, citing Xu et al. (2019); section 3.3 repeats this to establish that the generator loss depends only on the conditional vector sampled at random and is therefore independent of the real training data, which is the premise of Corollary 2; section 4.1 names the baselines as PATE-GAN and DP-WGAN only, and Tables 3-5 report no CTGAN row; the CTAB-GAN reference appears in the bibliography alone
needs: convention gap: CTGAN's conditional architecture is a structural component of the proposed model and load-bearing for its privacy proof, yet CTGAN is never named in prose, run, or benchmarked. Recorded citation_only 2 under the adopted-but-not-run rule; an inherited-architecture convention, if one is wanted, would place this higher

title: Detecting Malicious Accounts showing Adversarial Behavior in Permissionless Blockchains
summary: Flags accounts behind malicious activity in permissionless blockchains from temporal and behavioural transaction features, and then asks whether the resulting detectors survive accounts that have been altered to evade them. CTGAN generates that adversarial data: it is fitted separately on each malicious activity class with default parameters and 1000 epochs, and the generated accounts are added to the test set to measure how far detector performance falls.
evidence: Section 2 states that of the GAN variants only CTGan is described because it is the one used to generate fake data for every malicious activity, chosen because it generates tabular data, and records its two fully connected hidden layers, the authors' recommendation of more than 300 epochs, and the limitation that the generator needs at least 10 feature vectors; section 3.3 states CTGan is used to generate adversarial data Dg for the malicious activities and that Dg is used only on the test dataset, with default parameters and 1000 epochs for fitting; the paper spells the model CTGan throughout

title: Fed-TGAN: Federated Learning Framework for Synthesizing Tabular Data
summary: Presents a federated learning framework for training tabular GANs across clients that cannot pool their data, addressing the fact that tabular generators need per-column global statistics before a common encoding can be agreed: it builds the categorical and continuous encoders at the federator without seeing local rows, and weights client model updates by a table-similarity score alongside row count, converging faster than multi-discriminator and vanilla federated baselines on non-IID and quantity-skewed splits. CTGAN is the generator being federated in every arm of the evaluation, and the privacy-preserving encoder construction is written against CTGAN's own scheme, one-hot for categoricals and variational Gaussian mixture mode-specific normalization for continuous columns, with CTGAN's default settings retained.
evidence: the contributions list states the framework is for decentralized learning of tabular GANs, naming CTGAN, and that the authors apply Fed-TGAN with CTGAN as an example while claiming usage is not limited to it; section 2 states that TGAN, CTGAN and CTAB-GAN use one-hot encoding for categorical columns and variational Gaussian mixture encoding for continuous columns, which is the dependency the federated encoder is designed around; the experimental setup states the aim is to learn a CTGAN model from distributed clients using the three frameworks on the basis of CTGAN's default settings for encoding features, with 10 as the mode limit for the VGM encoders, and that all baselines were re-implemented in PyTorch 1.8.1 RPC. Importance 4 rather than 5 on the constrained-DGM precedent: CTGAN is the sole substrate actually run but is declared interchangeable, and its generator and losses are unmodified - what is extended is its encoding and training protocol.

title: Improving Model Compatibility of Generative Adversarial Networks by Boundary Calibration
summary: Adds a boundary-calibration loss to adversarial training that penalises generated points falling across decision boundaries approximated by classifiers pretrained on the real data, and reports that the resulting BWGAN and BMMDGAN raise the accuracy of models trained on synthetic data across four UCI tables and two image sets without losing sample quality. CTGAN supplies the machine-learning-efficacy criterion the paper adopts as its measure of model compatibility and is the tabular prior work it positions against, but it is not run.
evidence: the introduction names the target property model compatibility [24] or machine learning efficacy [32], where reference [32] is Xu, Skoularidou, Cuesta-Infante and Veeramachaneni, Modeling tabular data using conditional GAN, NeurIPS 2019, and credits [32] as the pioneering work showing conditional GANs give better model compatibility than VAEs; section 3 contrasts the proposed loss with Tabular GAN [32] and states the method applies to most GAN variants including it; the compared methods in section 5.1 are WGAN, MMD GAN and ACGAN with their BC-loss counterparts, and Tables 1 to 5 carry no CTGAN row

title: Accurate and Intuitive Contextual Explanations using Linear Model Trees
summary: Proposes LMTE, a local surrogate explainer that fits a linear model tree to synthetic data drawn around the test point, so that a single explanation carries both feature attributions and rules and can follow a non-linear decision boundary that a weighted linear surrogate cannot. CTGAN is the sampling stage the method is built on: the nearest neighbours of the test point are transformed, fed to CTGAN with the discrete columns declared, and the fitted model sampled to produce the locality the surrogate is trained on.
evidence: Table 1 lists the sampling method of the proposed approach as CTGAN, against uniform random for LIME and a genetic algorithm for LORE; section 3.1 states the transformed tabular data is fed to the CTGAN along with the discrete columns so that it can handle them separately, and that test points are sampled from the trained model to give the data generated around the test point's locality; section 3.2 states the synthetic neighbourhood is obtained from the CTGAN before the surrogate is fitted; Figure 3(b) plots the synthetic dataset generated by CTGAN with the decision boundary of the linear model tree fitted to it

title: Generation of Differentially Private Heterogeneous Electronic Health Records
summary: Explores generative adversarial training for synthetic electronic health records that mix binary, categorical and continuous administrative and diagnostic fields, selects a WGAN-GP formulation over MedGAN and WGAN on data-fidelity grounds, and then retrains it under (1, 1e-5) differential privacy, reporting a roughly 17% drop in downstream readmission-classification utility and a sub-population analysis showing no bias introduced beyond what the source data already carried. CTGAN was trained as a candidate generator and dropped for slow training and poorer results on the paper's high-cardinality discrete features, but its mode-specific normalization is retained: the real-valued columns are decomposed with Gaussian mixture models as in CTGAN before the surviving WGAN-GP model is fitted.
evidence: section 2.1 describes CTGAN as introducing mode-specific normalization and conditional training by sampling to combat mode collapse on tabular data; section 3.1 states that the real-valued features are decomposed using Gaussian Mixture Models as is done in the CTGAN, as part of the preprocessing feeding the model that is actually used; section 3.2 records a preliminary investigation into using the CTGAN model whose large number of discrete features led to markedly increased training time and poorer results, so the CTGAN itself is not included as a potential model. Importance 4 rather than 3 under the convention that a paper both comparing CTGAN and building on its mode-specific normalization moves up a step; note that the comparison rests on that prose sentence, as CTGAN has no row in Table 1 or Table 2 (MedGAN, WGAN, WGAN-GP only), so a reviewer preferring the results-row test would record 3.

title: Improving the Reconstruction of Disentangled Representation Learners via Multi-Stage Modeling
summary: Splits disentangled representation learning into two stages, a penalty-based model that infers independent factors and a second conditional model that recovers the correlated residual, so reconstruction quality is regained without weakening disentanglement, and shows the construction can be realised with variational autoencoders, adversarial networks or normalising flows. A closing section carries the method to simulated credit tabular data, where TVAE is one of two benchmark generators trained against it and its mode-specific normalization is set out as the reference treatment of mixed continuous and discrete columns.

title: Synthesising artificial patient-level data for Open Science - an evaluation of five methods
summary: Asks whether patient-level data can be published for open science without compromising confidentiality, and evaluates five synthesis methods against that bar. CTGAN produces the structured tabular arm, an early appearance of the architecture in the open-science framing rather than the machine-learning one.
evidence: abstract: CT-GAN used to produce structured tabular synthetic patient data

title: Synthetic Data -- Anonymisation Groundhog Day
summary: Measures the privacy gain of publishing synthetic data by running the same linkage and attribute-inference games against synthetic datasets and against traditionally sanitised releases, and concludes that synthetic data either fails to stop the attacks or loses the utility it was meant to preserve, with the gain varying so widely from record to record that it cannot be promised in advance. CTGAN is one of the five generative models the attacks are run against, and is the deep tabular generator carried through the headline per-record results.

title: Effective and Privacy Preserving Tabular Data Synthesizing
summary: A Delft master's thesis that first compares four GAN-based tabular synthesizers on machine learning utility, statistical similarity and privacy, then proposes CTAB-GAN, a conditional table GAN adding a mixed-type encoder, classification and information losses and a DCGAN backbone, and finally extends it to DP-CTABGAN with differentially private training evaluated under membership and attribute inference attacks. CTAB-GAN is built on CTGAN: its mixed-type encoder is derived from CTGAN's mode-specific normalization and it adopts CTGAN's conditional vector and training-by-sampling, while CTGAN is separately one of the four benchmarked baselines, run from the sdv-dev/SDGym code base.
evidence: Section 4.2 states that in CTAB-GAN a Mixed-type Encoder is invented based on the mode-specific normalization introduced in the work of [43], that CTAB-GAN is based on a conditional GAN and utilizes training-by-sampling to treat imbalanced variables, and that it features the classification, information and generator losses; section 2.2.1 reproduces CTGAN's conditional vector construction, generator cross-entropy loss and training-by-sampling procedure in full and attributes all three to [43]; section 2.1.1 credits CTGAN with the conditional architecture, training-by-sampling and mode-specific normalization while noting it cannot handle missing values; section 3.2.2 lists CTGAN as one of four evaluated state-of-the-art baselines, with a footnote giving https://github.com/sdv-dev/SDGym as the code base for all the models; reference [43] resolves to Xu, Skoularidou, Cuesta-Infante and Veeramachaneni
